results.summary: This project implements a perceptron neuron in Verilog that is trained to produce a NAND gate function. It has eight input pins for the current bit, eight output pins for the state variable bits, and one bidirectional pin for the output bit. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of placeholder sections, so it is unclear how the training is performed or how the design is used. The design is notable for demonstrating a basic neural network element in hardware, but without detailed documentation, its operation and intended use are ambiguous.

This design implements a hardware PID controller in Verilog. It takes an 8-bit setpoint and an 8-bit feedback signal as inputs and produces an 8-bit control signal output. The controller uses proportional, integral, and derivative terms to adjust the output based on the error between setpoint and feedback, but it only outputs positive values, making it suitable for systems that naturally tend in one direction, such as heating. The design is intended for simulation testing and can be deployed with sensors and actuators for real-world control applications.

This project is an 8-bit prefix network-based adder designed with the aid of a large language model to achieve a balance between power, performance, and area. It takes two 8-bit operands (a and b) and produces an 8-bit sum output. The design uses specific modules (Square, BigCircle, SmallCircle, Triangle) to generate carries and sums. The test procedure applies all possible input combinations and verifies the sum against the expected result, ensuring correct functionality.

This project implements a synchronous 4-bit counter with control signals for counting, loading, and output enable. The counter increments on each clock cycle when the count enable is asserted, can load a 4-bit value when the load enable is asserted, and can be disabled to put the output in high-impedance. It includes a reset that clears the counter to zero. The design is tested by observing the output on dedicated pins while manipulating the control signals to verify counting, pausing, loading, and output disabling.

This project implements a basic leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron in SystemVerilog. It integrates input current by addition and leaks by dividing by two at each time step, with an enable pin advancing time roughly once per second when clocked at about 50 MHz. The neuron fires a spike when the integrated value exceeds a threshold, and it includes a timeout to prevent constant output from overstimulation. Testing involves manually setting input switches to provide current and observing spike output on LEDs, with a dedicated LED indicating time steps.

This project is a general-purpose UART with FIFO buffers, developed by Purdue's SoCET team. It supports standard UART signals (rx, tx, cts, rts) and includes FIFO buffers for both transmit and receive paths. The design allows configuration of baud rate and operation mode (idle, transmit, receive, buffer clear) through control pins. It can be tested by connecting to another UART or a USB-to-serial adapter, and it provides error and buffer status flags.

This design is a versatile PWM generator with adjustable frequency and duty cycle. It takes a 6-bit divisor input to set the frequency by dividing the clock, and two control inputs to increase or decrease the duty cycle by 10% steps. The PWM output can be used to drive RGB LEDs, servomotors, and other devices, but external power is recommended for the driven device. The design is intended to be tested by applying a clock, setting the divisor, and adjusting the duty cycle while observing the PWM output.

This is a simple 4-bit R2R digital-to-analog converter implemented as an analog design. It accepts a 4-bit digital input on pins A0 to A3 and produces an analog output voltage on a single output pin. The design is tested by applying a sequence of digital codes from 0000 to 1111 and observing the corresponding analog output, typically with an ADALM2000 in digital mode. The converter provides a basic method to generate analog signals from digital values.

This project is a test chip for a 3-stage PMOS operational amplifier. It provides three analog pins: an output, an inverting input, and a non-inverting input. The design is intended to be tested with a typical analog bench setup, likely to characterize its performance such as gain and bandwidth. The documentation is minimal, indicating it is primarily a test vehicle for the amplifier topology.

The Styler chip manipulates 16x16 character glyph bitmaps based on text mode attributes such as bold, faint, italic, underline, and blink. It has registers for scanline, control, bitmap, and attributes, and it interfaces via 8 bidirectional data pins and several control inputs. The typical use involves writing a scanline number, reading back a logical scanline, and then manipulating bitmap halves to apply visual effects. The chip is intended as part of a larger text mode video display hardware system, and testing is covered by provided test scripts.
